authoring_notes: Authored for the api-call branch learning schema and the existing Domain 3 question bundle. Uses CompTIA's official objective IDs 3.1-3.4 as skill IDs because the bullet examples under each objective are not separately numbered. Content is definition-first, keeps tables mobile-friendly at no more than three columns, teaches the exact concept IDs used by Domain 3 questions, and treats architecture choices as scenario-dependent tradeoffs rather than universal rules. Supporting claims were checked against NIST and IETF references where appropriate.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: Who secures what in cloud computing?

reveal.text: Cloud use changes who performs security tasks; it does not remove the customer's responsibilities. The exact boundary depends on the service model and contract.

spans.text: does not remove the customer's responsibilities

columns.title: Provider side
items: Secures the cloud service and the infrastructure it operates.
Responsibilities vary by service model.

columns.title: Customer side
items: Secures what it deploys, configures, stores, and grants access to.
Data, identities, and configuration remain important customer concerns.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Serverless and microservices?

reveal.text: Serverless lets you run code while the provider manages more of the underlying server platform. Microservices split an application into smaller services that communicate through APIs or network calls.

spans.text: provider manages more of the underlying server platform

prompts.label: KEEP THEM SEPARATE
prompts.placeholder: How are these architectures different?

cells.meaning: Provider runs the underlying execution platform; code runs on demand.
cells.security: Secure code, identities, data, configuration, dependencies, and event triggers.

cells.meaning: Application is split into small independently deployable services.
cells.security: Authenticate and authorize service calls; protect APIs and service-to-service traffic.

reveal.text: Serverless does not mean 'no servers'; it means the provider manages more of the server platform. Microservices increase the number of service identities, APIs, and network relationships that must be secured.

spans.text: provider manages more of the server platform
service identities, APIs, and network relationships

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Physical isolation, segmentation, and SDN?

reveal.text: Physical isolation removes or restricts a physical network path. Logical segmentation controls which systems may communicate, while software-defined networking (SDN) uses software-controlled policy to manage network behavior.

prompts.label: THREE MODELS
prompts.placeholder: Compare the isolation approaches.

cells.idea: No direct network connection to less-trusted networks.
cells.watch: Strong separation, but removable media and maintenance paths can still introduce risk.

cells.idea: Uses logical controls such as VLANs, routing, and firewalls to separate traffic.
cells.watch: Depends on correct configuration and enforcement.

cells.idea: Network behavior is centrally controlled through software.
cells.watch: Policy can be automated, but the management/control layer becomes high-value.

reveal.text: Ask two questions: 'Is there a physical path?' and 'What policy controls the logical path?' Air-gapped systems remove a direct network path; segmentation and SDN control allowed paths.

glossary.definition: The management logic that decides how network traffic should be handled; protecting it is important because it can influence many devices at once.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about On-premises, centralized, and decentralized designs?

reveal.text: Centralized designs concentrate services or control in fewer locations. Decentralized designs spread them across more locations or components, changing failure, management, and security tradeoffs.

spans.text: spread them across more locations or components

prompts.label: TRADEOFF
prompts.placeholder: What changes with centralization?

columns.title: Centralized
items: Consistent policy and visibility can be easier.
A central service can become a critical dependency and concentrated target.

columns.title: Decentralized
items: Can reduce dependence on one control point.
Coordination, policy consistency, and monitoring can become harder.

prompts.label: ON-PREMISES
prompts.placeholder: Where does on-premises fit?

reveal.text: In an on-premises design, the organization operates systems in facilities it controls and therefore carries more direct responsibility for hardware, power, physical security, patching, and operations.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Containerization and virtualization?

reveal.text: Containers package applications with their dependencies while commonly sharing the host operating-system kernel. Virtual machines use a hypervisor and normally run separate guest operating systems.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: What is the isolation boundary?

cells.boundary: Processes share the host OS kernel while using isolation features.
cells.implication: Host/kernel security and container runtime configuration are critical.

cells.boundary: Each VM runs its own guest OS on a hypervisor.
cells.implication: The hypervisor and VM configuration form an important isolation boundary.

reveal.text: Containers are not the same isolation model as full virtual machines. Containers commonly share the host kernel, while VMs normally have separate guest operating systems.

nodes.title: IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, and embedded systems

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, and embedded systems?

reveal.text: IoT, ICS/SCADA, real-time operating systems, and embedded systems often interact with physical devices or operate under strict resource, timing, safety, or availability constraints.

spans.text: resource, timing, safety, or availability constraints

prompts.label: KNOW THE ENVIRONMENT
prompts.placeholder: What makes each system special?

cells.purpose: Network-connected sensors, appliances, and smart devices.
cells.security: Large device counts, limited resources, long lifecycles, and uneven patch support.

cells.type: Industrial control systems (ICS) / supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)
cells.purpose: Monitor or control physical and industrial processes.
cells.security: Safety and availability can be as important as confidentiality; changes may require careful testing and downtime planning.

cells.purpose: Respond to events within predictable timing constraints.
cells.security: Security controls must not break required timing behavior.

cells.purpose: Dedicated computing built into a device.
cells.security: Limited compute, vendor dependence, and long service life may constrain updates and controls.

prompts.label: DESIGN RULE
prompts.placeholder: How should you secure constrained systems?

reveal.text: Start with the system's safety, availability, timing, patchability, power, and compute limits. When direct patching or endpoint controls are impractical, reduce exposure with segmentation, access restrictions, monitoring, and other compensating controls.

prompts.placeholder: What is high availability?

reveal.text: High availability keeps a service usable despite component failures. It reduces single points of failure by using redundant capacity, clustering, load balancing, or failover paths.

prompts.label: LOOK FOR
prompts.placeholder: What design clues suggest HA?

items: redundant components
health checks
failover
multiple instances
multiple paths

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 — Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Architecture security tradeoffs?

reveal.text: Architecture choices trade off security, availability, cost, performance, scalability, deployment speed, and recovery. Start with the scenario's most important requirement before choosing a design.

prompts.label: TRADEOFFS
prompts.placeholder: Which architecture question is being asked?

cells.question: Can service continue through failure, and recover quickly?
What do redundancy, operations, licenses, and staffing cost?
Does the design meet latency or time-sensitive needs?
Can capacity grow without redesigning everything?
How safely and consistently can changes be released?
Which financial or operational risk is shifted by contract, insurance, or outsourcing?
How hard is it to rebuild or restore the service?

reveal.text: There is rarely one architecture that maximizes security, cost, speed, and availability at the same time. Identify the scenario's priority first, then choose the design whose tradeoff matches it.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 — Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

nodes.title: Patch availability, power, and compute constraints

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Patch availability, power, and compute constraints?

reveal.text: Some systems cannot be patched easily or have limited power and compute capacity. Those constraints can prevent standard security controls, so compensating protections may be needed.

prompts.label: CONSTRAINTS
prompts.placeholder: What can prevent a normal security control?

items: No vendor patch is available
A patch cannot be applied without unsafe downtime or compatibility risk
The device has too little CPU, memory, or storage for heavy security software
Battery or power limits make continuous processing impractical

prompts.label: WHEN YOU CANNOT PATCH
prompts.placeholder: What should you do?

items: Reduce exposure and reachable paths
Restrict access to only required identities and systems
Add monitoring or filtering around the constrained system
Plan a tested maintenance, replacement, or upgrade path

prompts.placeholder: Why does placement matter?

reveal.text: A security zone groups systems with similar trust and exposure. Place systems and controls so higher-risk traffic crosses an enforcement boundary before it can reach more sensitive resources.

items: Internet or untrusted network
Public-facing zone
Application or service zone

NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 — Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

prompts.label: WHAT
prompts.placeholder: What is the attack surface?

reveal.text: The attack surface is the set of reachable interfaces, services, accounts, paths, and dependencies an attacker could target. Unnecessary exposure creates more opportunities for attack.

spans.text: reachable interfaces, services, accounts, paths, and dependencies

prompts.label: REDUCE IT
prompts.placeholder: What should you change?

items: Close or block unused ports and services
Limit inbound and outbound paths
Avoid direct administrative access from untrusted networks
Expose only the systems and protocols required by the business need

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 — Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Fail-open and fail-closed?

reveal.text: Fail-open allows access or traffic to continue when a control fails. Fail-closed blocks access or traffic on failure, favoring security over availability.

spans.text: blocks access or traffic on failure

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: What happens when the control fails?

columns.title: Fail-open
items: Traffic or access continues when the control fails.
Favors availability, but may reduce protection during failure.

columns.title: Fail-closed
items: Traffic or access is blocked when the control fails.
Favors protection, but may interrupt legitimate service.

prompts.label: EXAM CLUE
prompts.placeholder: How do you choose?

reveal.text: Choose the failure mode from the scenario's priority. A life-safety or availability requirement can change the answer; a highly sensitive boundary may justify blocking access on failure.

nodes.title: Active, passive, inline, and monitor-mode devices

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Active, passive, inline, and monitor-mode devices?

reveal.text: Active and passive describe whether a device can act on traffic. Inline and monitor/tap describe whether the device sits directly in the traffic path or observes a copy.

spans.text: sits directly in the traffic path

prompts.label: TWO DIMENSIONS
prompts.placeholder: Classify device behavior.

cells.meaning: Can take action that changes or blocks traffic.
cells.risk: Can prevent attacks, but incorrect action can disrupt traffic.

cells.meaning: Observes and reports without directly changing traffic.
cells.risk: Lower risk of blocking valid traffic.
The device can become part of the availability path.

cells.meaning: Receives a copy of traffic out of band.
cells.risk: Good visibility without becoming the forwarding path.

reveal.text: Active does not always mean inline, and passive does not always mean tap. 'Active/passive' describes behavior; 'inline/monitor' describes placement in the traffic path.

spans.text: describes placement in the traffic path

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Jump servers and proxy servers?

reveal.text: A jump server is a controlled system used for administrative access to protected resources. A proxy intermediates client traffic to another destination.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: Which intermediary is this?

columns.title: Jump server
items: Controlled administrative entry point to restricted systems.
Reduces the number of systems that accept direct admin connections.

columns.title: Proxy server
items: Intermediary that makes requests or connections on behalf of a client.
Can filter, inspect, log, or hide direct client-to-destination communication.

reveal.text: If the problem is privileged administration, think jump server. If the problem is brokering client traffic to another destination, think proxy.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 — Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

nodes.title: Intrusion detection system (IDS) and intrusion prevention system (IPS)

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Intrusion detection system (IDS) and intrusion prevention system (IPS)?

reveal.text: An intrusion detection system (IDS) detects suspicious traffic and alerts. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) can also block matching malicious traffic, usually because it operates inline.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: Detect or block?

columns.title: Intrusion detection system (IDS)
items: Detects suspicious activity and generates alerts.
Often deployed for visibility without directly blocking traffic.

columns.title: Intrusion prevention system (IPS)
items: Detects and can prevent or block malicious traffic.
Often placed inline when it must stop traffic.

prompts.label: WHEN
prompts.placeholder: Which one fits?

reveal.text: Choose IDS when visibility is the main goal and blocking risk must be minimized. Choose IPS when the control must automatically stop matching malicious traffic and the availability impact is acceptable.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Load balancers and sensors?

reveal.text: A load balancer distributes traffic across service instances. A sensor observes activity and produces telemetry for monitoring or analysis.

prompts.label: DIFFERENT JOBS
prompts.placeholder: What does each appliance do?

columns.title: Load balancer
items: Distributes client requests across multiple service instances.
Supports capacity and availability; health checks can avoid failed instances.

columns.title: Sensor
items: Collects telemetry about network, system, or environmental activity.
Provides observations for monitoring, detection, or analysis.

reveal.text: A load balancer is not automatically a firewall or intrusion-prevention system. Its primary role is traffic distribution unless additional security functions are explicitly present.

reveal.text: 802.1X provides port-based network access control: a device or user must authenticate before normal access is granted. EAP is the framework commonly used to carry the authentication exchange.

items: Supplicant: the connecting user/device
Authenticator: the switch or access point controlling the port
Authentication server: validates the authentication method and result

glossary.definition: The client device or software requesting network access during 802.1X authentication.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Firewall types and inspection layers?

reveal.text: A firewall enforces network traffic policy. Different firewall types inspect different layers or combine additional security functions, so the required visibility determines the best fit.

prompts.label: CHOOSE BY WHAT YOU MUST INSPECT
prompts.placeholder: Compare firewall types.

cells.clue: Injection, malicious web requests, public web app.

cells.focus: Multiple security functions combined in one platform.
cells.clue: Consolidated firewall, filtering, malware or intrusion features.

cells.focus: Firewalling plus deeper application/user-aware inspection features.
IP addresses, transport protocols, and ports.
cells.clue: Allow TCP 443; block a source network or port.
Inspect HTTP methods, URLs, application behavior, or content.

reveal.text: Pick the narrowest control that sees the information needed for the decision. A Layer 4 rule cannot inspect an HTTP request body; a WAF is designed specifically for web application traffic.

prompts.label: WHAT
prompts.placeholder: What problem does a VPN solve?

reveal.text: A virtual private network creates a protected tunnel across an untrusted network so remote users or sites can communicate with private resources more securely.

prompts.label: REMOTE ACCESS DESIGN
prompts.placeholder: What else is needed besides encryption?

Authorize only the resources required

nodes.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Internet Protocol Security (IPsec)

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Internet Protocol Security (IPsec)?

reveal.text: Transport Layer Security (TLS) protects application sessions such as HTTPS. Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) protects IP traffic and is commonly used for network-to-network or host-to-network secure tunnels.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: Where is the protection applied?

columns.title: TLS
items: Protects an application connection between endpoints, commonly over TCP.
Common example: HTTPS.

columns.title: IPsec
items: Protects IP traffic at the network layer.
Common use: host-to-host or site-to-site protected IP communication.

reveal.text: A browser-to-web-service secure session points toward TLS. A persistent encrypted tunnel between network gateways points toward IPsec.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about SD-WAN and SASE?

reveal.text: Software-defined wide area networking (SD-WAN) centrally manages and steers WAN paths. Secure access service edge (SASE) combines connectivity with cloud-delivered security services closer to users and applications.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: Networking or networking plus cloud security?

columns.title: SD-WAN
items: Software-defined management and path selection across WAN links.
Focus: connecting sites and optimizing WAN traffic.

columns.title: SASE
items: Converges WAN connectivity with cloud-delivered security services.
Focus: secure access for distributed users, sites, and applications.

reveal.text: If the scenario mainly asks how to steer and manage WAN paths, think SD-WAN. If it combines distributed connectivity with security services delivered from the cloud edge, think SASE.

spans.text: security services delivered from the cloud edge

correct placement
right inspection layer
secure administration
encrypted remote access
monitoring plus prevention
failure behavior

modules.title: Protect data by type, state, and location

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Recognize data types?

reveal.text: A data type describes what information is or why it matters, such as regulated, intellectual property, financial, or human-readable business data. It is different from a handling classification.

spans.text: what information is or why it matters

prompts.label: DATA TYPE
prompts.placeholder: What kind of data is it?

cells.meaning: Handling is governed by an applicable law or regulation.
cells.example: Data with legally mandated protection or retention.

cells.meaning: Confidential business information that derives value from remaining secret.
Creations or proprietary knowledge with legal or business value.
cells.example: Source code, designs, patents, copyrighted works.

cells.meaning: Information created or retained for legal matters.
Information about money, transactions, accounts, or financial operations.
A person can directly interpret the content.
cells.example: Plain text or a visible report.

cells.meaning: A specialized parser, decoder, or application is needed to interpret it.

reveal.text: Data type describes what the information is or why it matters. It is different from a classification label, which is an organization's handling label.

prompts.label: CLASSIFICATION
prompts.placeholder: What does a classification label do?

reveal.text: A data classification label communicates required handling based on sensitivity, business impact, or policy. Security+ lists labels such as sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private, and critical.

prompts.label: IMPORTANT
prompts.placeholder: Is there one universal ranking?

reveal.text: Do not assume every organization ranks these labels in the same order. Use the policy and scenario to determine what each label means and which controls it requires.

nodes.title: Data at rest, in transit, and in use

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Data at rest, in transit, and in use?

reveal.text: Data can be at rest in storage, in transit across a network, or in use while being processed. The protection must match the state.

prompts.label: THREE STATES
prompts.placeholder: Where is the data right now?

cells.meaning: Stored and not actively moving between systems.
Moving across a network or communication channel.
cells.example: API request, file transfer, VPN traffic.

cells.meaning: Actively processed or accessed by a running system.
cells.example: Data in application memory while being processed.

reveal.text: Match the protection to the state: storage controls and encryption for data at rest, protected protocols for data in transit, and strong access/process isolation for data in use.

nodes.title: Data sovereignty, geolocation, and geographic restrictions

prompts.label: LOCATION MATTERS
prompts.placeholder: What is data sovereignty?

reveal.text: Data sovereignty means data can be subject to legal or regulatory requirements based on the jurisdiction connected to where it is stored or processed. Geolocation identifies where systems or data are located.

spans.text: where it is stored or processed

items: Identify the applicable location or jurisdiction requirement
Choose approved regions or facilities
Restrict replication, backup, and processing to allowed locations

glossary.definition: The legal authority whose laws or regulations apply to a person, organization, activity, or location.

nodes.title: Encryption and hashing for data protection

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Encryption and hashing for data protection?

reveal.text: Encryption protects confidentiality by making data unreadable without the required key. Hashing produces a digest mainly used to detect change or support integrity checks.

columns.title: Encryption
items: Transforms data using a cryptographic key so unauthorized parties cannot read it.
Primary goal here: confidentiality.

columns.title: Hashing
items: Produces a fixed-size digest from data.
Useful for detecting changes or comparing values; it does not hide the original data by itself.

reveal.text: If the requirement says 'keep the contents secret,' hashing alone is not enough. If the requirement says 'detect whether this value changed,' a cryptographic hash may be appropriate.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Masking, tokenization, and obfuscation?

reveal.text: Masking hides part of a value from a viewer. Tokenization replaces sensitive data with a substitute token, while obfuscation makes information harder to understand.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: How is the sensitive value changed?

cells.idea: Hide or replace part or all of a displayed value.
cells.clue: Show only the last four digits.

cells.idea: Replace a sensitive value with a non-sensitive token; the original value is kept separately or recoverable through the token system.
cells.clue: Applications use a surrogate value instead of the real identifier.

cells.idea: Make information or code harder to understand.
cells.clue: Discourage easy interpretation; not a substitute for strong encryption when secrecy is required.

reveal.text: Masking changes what a viewer sees. Tokenization substitutes a different value for the sensitive one. Obfuscation makes interpretation harder, but does not automatically provide cryptographic confidentiality.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Data segmentation and permission restrictions?

reveal.text: Segmentation limits which systems can reach data. Permission restrictions limit which identities are authorized to use it; strong protection often needs both.

prompts.label: TWO BARRIERS
prompts.placeholder: How do these controls differ?

columns.title: Segmentation
items: Separates systems, datasets, or paths so compromise in one area does not automatically expose another.
Think: isolate where data can be reached from.

columns.title: Permission restrictions
items: Limit which identities or processes can read, change, delete, or administer data.
Think: limit who can do what.

reveal.text: Protect sensitive data with both reachability limits and authorization limits. 'Can this system reach the data?' and 'Is this identity allowed to use it?' are separate questions.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Load balancing and clustering?

reveal.text: Load balancing distributes requests across service instances. Clustering coordinates multiple systems so they can act as one service and support availability or failover.

prompts.label: HIGH AVAILABILITY
prompts.placeholder: Compare the mechanisms.

columns.title: Load balancing
items: Distributes requests or connections across multiple service instances.
Can avoid unhealthy instances and spread demand.

columns.title: Clustering
items: Multiple systems coordinate to provide a service and can support failover or shared availability.
The nodes act as a coordinated service group.

reveal.text: A system can use both clustering and load balancing. The exam clue is the primary function being described: traffic distribution versus coordinated service/failover.

nodes.title: Hot, warm, and cold recovery sites

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Hot, warm, and cold recovery sites?

reveal.text: Recovery sites are alternate locations prepared to restore operations after disruption. Hot, warm, and cold sites mainly differ in readiness, recovery speed, and ongoing cost.

spans.text: readiness, recovery speed, and ongoing cost

prompts.label: RECOVERY SITE
prompts.placeholder: How ready is the alternate site?

cells.readiness: Systems, connectivity, and data are prepared for rapid operation.
cells.tradeoff: Fast recovery; highest ongoing cost and maintenance.

cells.readiness: Some systems and connectivity are prepared; additional restore or configuration is needed.
cells.tradeoff: Middle ground for cost and recovery time.

cells.readiness: Facility and basic resources exist, but systems/data need significant setup or restoration.

reveal.text: When a scenario demands the shortest recovery time and accepts higher cost, a hot site is the usual fit. When cost matters more than recovery speed, warm or cold options may fit better.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Geographic and platform diversity?

reveal.text: Diversity reduces dependence on one location, provider, platform, or implementation. It can reduce correlated failures but increases operational complexity.

columns.title: Geographic dispersion
items: Places redundant resources far enough apart to reduce shared location disasters and utility failures.

columns.title: Platform diversity
items: Uses different platforms or technologies to reduce dependence on one shared implementation or failure mode.

reveal.text: Diversity can reduce correlated failures, but it adds operational complexity, training needs, integration work, and more configurations to secure.

glossary.definition: A failure that affects multiple redundant components because they share the same underlying dependency, location, provider, or defect.

prompts.label: MULTI-CLOUD
prompts.placeholder: Does two providers automatically mean resilience?

reveal.text: A multi-cloud design uses services from more than one cloud provider. It only adds failover value when data, identity, networking, operations, and recovery are designed to work across providers.

Continuity of operations keeps essential functions available or restores them during disruption. Architecture supports this with alternate capacity, documented recovery paths, trained people, and tested procedures.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Capacity planning for resilience?

reveal.text: Capacity planning ensures enough people, technology, network, power, facilities, and other resources are available to sustain normal and recovery operations.

spans.text: enough people, technology, network, power, facilities

prompts.label: THREE CAPACITIES
prompts.placeholder: What must be available during normal operation and recovery?

cells.question: Are enough trained responders, operators, and decision-makers available?
Are compute, storage, software, licenses, and services sufficient?
Are network, facilities, power, and supporting resources sufficient?

reveal.text: Recovery capacity is not only CPU and storage. A technically redundant system can still fail operationally if trained people, network capacity, power, licenses, or facilities are missing.

spans.text: trained people, network capacity, power, licenses, or facilities

nodes.title: Tabletop, failover, simulation, and parallel testing

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Tabletop, failover, simulation, and parallel testing?

reveal.text: Resilience testing checks whether recovery plans, people, and technical failover actually work. Tabletop, simulation, failover, and parallel tests provide different levels of realism and operational risk.

spans.text: recovery plans, people, and technical failover

prompts.label: TEST TYPE
prompts.placeholder: What is actually happening?

cells.action: Participants discuss a scenario and walk through decisions without switching production.
Service is transferred to the alternate system or site to verify it can take over.
A realistic event is exercised in a controlled way without necessarily disrupting production.
cells.clue: Practice the response under simulated conditions.

cells.action: Primary and alternate processing run at the same time so results/capability can be compared.

reveal.text: A plan you never test is only an assumption. Use low-risk exercises to find procedural gaps, then progressively test technical failover and recovery where business risk allows.

glossary.definition: The point when production service or workload is switched from one environment to another.

nodes.title: Backup strategy: location, frequency, encryption, snapshots

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Backup strategy: location, frequency, encryption, snapshots?

reveal.text: A backup strategy defines how often recoverable copies are created, where they are stored, how they are protected, and how restoration will be tested.

spans.text: how often recoverable copies are created

prompts.label: BACKUP DESIGN
prompts.placeholder: What decisions matter?

cells.why: Offsite copies reduce the chance that one site disaster destroys production and every backup.
More frequent recoverable copies reduce the amount of recent work that may be lost.
Backups can contain the same sensitive data as production and require confidentiality protection.
Point-in-time copies can speed recovery, but their failure domain and retention must be understood.

reveal.text: Do not treat a snapshot as automatically equivalent to an independent offsite backup. Ask where the copy lives, whether the same failure can destroy it, whether it is protected, and whether restoration has been tested.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Replication and journaling?

reveal.text: Replication copies data or system state to another location or system. Journaling records changes or transactions so a prior state can be reconstructed or replayed.

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: Copy state or record changes?

columns.title: Replication
items: Copies data or system state to another location or system.
Supports availability and recovery, often with low delay.

columns.title: Journaling
items: Records changes or transactions so state can be reconstructed or replayed.
Useful for point-in-time recovery and understanding the sequence of changes.

reveal.text: Replication is not a replacement for protected backups. A deletion, corruption, or bad change may also replicate unless separate recovery points are retained.

spans.text: not a replacement for protected backups

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) and generators?

reveal.text: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) provides immediate short-term power during an outage. A generator can provide longer-duration power but needs startup time, fuel, maintenance, and testing.

prompts.label: POWER CONTROLS
prompts.placeholder: What does each one provide?

columns.title: UPS
items: Battery-backed power starts immediately when utility power is interrupted.
Bridges short outages or the startup time of longer-duration power.

columns.title: Generator
items: Produces power for longer outages once started and supplied with fuel.
Supports extended operation but normally takes time to start.

reveal.text: Think 'UPS now, generator longer.' A resilient facility also plans fuel, maintenance, testing, safe shutdown, and the power needs of network and cooling systems.
